cards.headline: A quote screen is a dozen answers, not one number.
cards.body: The last price gets all the attention. Everything around it — the ranges, the volume, the ratios — is context that tells you how the price got there and how much it means. Learn the fields once and every brokerage screen reads the same.

cards.headline: Last price, change, previous close.
cards.body: Northwind Robotics last traded at $48.20, up $3.20 or **7.11%**. Change is always measured from yesterday's closing price — $45.00 here. The percentage matters more than the dollars: $3.20 is loud on a $45 stock and noise on a $450 one.

cards.title: One week of Northwind Robotics
cards.caption: Yesterday closed at $45.00. Today opened at $46.50, ranged $46.10 to $48.90, and sits at $48.20 — still inside a 52-week band that runs $31.40 to $52.60.

cards.headline: The gap is where the news happened.
cards.body: Regular hours run 9:30 to 4:00 Eastern. Earnings, deals and headlines often land outside them, and pre-market trading reprices the stock before the opening bell. Northwind closed at $45.00 and opened at $46.50 — that $1.50 moved while the main session was shut.

cards.title: Volume against its average
cards.caption: Northwind normally trades about 1.2 million shares a day. Today it traded 4.8 million. Volume is the headcount behind a move — how many owners actually changed their minds.

cards.prompt: Two stocks each jump 7% today. One trades four times its average volume, the other a quarter of it. Which move has more conviction behind it?
cards.explanation: Heavy volume means a **crowd** repriced the stock. A big move on thin volume can be a handful of orders in a quiet market, and it often fades once normal trading returns.

cards.body: Three fields describe the business, not today's trading. Fifty million Northwind shares at $48.20 make it a $2.4 billion company. Its $0.96 annual dividend is 2.0% of that price.
Northwind earned $2.20 per share last year and trades at $48.20. Divide price by [[1]] and you get a P/E of 22 — the price of one dollar of yearly profit.
cards.explanation: A P/E is a comparison tool, not a verdict. Twenty-two only means something next to the company's own history, its rivals, and how fast its profits are growing.

cards.summary: A quote page answers three separate questions: what the price is, how much conviction sits behind it, and what the business costs.
bullets: Change is measured from yesterday's close, so an opening gap is news that traded without you.
Volume is conviction — a large move on thin volume is a weak signal.
Market cap, P/E and dividend yield describe the company, and only mean something next to a comparison.

cards.insight: A quote tells you what the market decided today. It never tells you whether the market was right.
